# Rabies

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Infectious diseases > Infections of the central nervous system > Rabies*

[Original Article Link](/library/Gh0B2f)

---

## Summary

Rabies is a <u>neurotropic</u> <u>virus</u> transmitted through the bite of an infected animal. The <u>virus</u> enters via the animal saliva, traveling along <u>peripheral nerves</u> to the <u>central nervous system</u> (<u>CNS</u>). The onset of nonspecific <u>flu-like symptoms</u> begins after an <u>incubation period</u> of 4–12 weeks, progressing to acute <u>rabies encephalitis</u>. Clinical features include <u>fever</u>, <u>hydrophobia</u>, <u>hypersalivation</u>, <u>stupor</u>, and <u>mania</u>, followed by <u>coma</u> and <u>death</u> resulting from respiratory and circulatory collapse. <u>Paralytic rabies</u>, a less common form, manifests with ascending <u>paralysis</u> that resembles <u>Guillain-Barré syndrome</u>. Rabies is preventable with <u>rabies postexposure prophylaxis</u> (PEP) and proper <u>wound care</u> but is almost always fatal once symptoms appear. <u>Rabies preexposure prophylaxis</u> (PrEP) is recommended for those at increased risk of exposure (e.g., veterinarians and travelers to <u>endemic</u> areas).

---

## Epidemiology

* Found in animal reservoirs in most countries throughout the world

* Considerable divide between developed and developing countries in terms of human deaths due to rabies

* <u>Incidence</u> worldwide: ∼ 60,000 people die of rabies each year.  [[1]](/library/VEdGu70)

* <u>Incidence</u> in the US: Three people on average die of rabies each year.





![Rabies fact sheet and mortality map](media/eo830i1j9seq6k6b8zgl8pvi.jpg)

Rabies fact sheet and mortality map




Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

* <u>Pathogen</u>

* Rabies is caused by several different members of the <u>Rhabdoviridae</u> family.

* <u>Rhabdoviruses</u> are rod or bullet shaped

* Genus: Lyssavirus

* ssRNA

* Transmission [[2]](/library/srdtir0)

* Most common animal reservoir worldwide: dogs (≥ 90%)

* Most common animal reservoirs in the US: bats, raccoons, skunks, and foxes

* Spread through saliva of rabid animal after bite injury

* Via aerosols (e.g., bat caves); rare





![Rabid dog](media/cqo73pkphrv7gsn8yqrb7ig6.jpg)

Rabid dog

---

## Pathophysiology

* <u>Rabies virus</u> binds the <u>ACh</u> <u>receptor</u> of <u>peripheral nerves</u> in the bite wound → migrates retrogradely along the axonal <u>microtubules</u> (using motor protein <u>dynein</u>) → enters the <u>CNS</u> → infects the <u>brain</u> [[3]](/library/13Y2hK)

* <u>Diencephalon</u>, <u>hippocampus</u>, and <u>brainstem</u> are involved first

* Causes acute, progressive, and fatal <u>encephalitis</u> → <u>encephalitic rabies</u>

* Causes ascending <u>flaccid paralysis</u> → <u>paralytic rabies</u>

---

## Clinical features

### General




* <u>Incubation period</u>: 4–12 weeks average  [[1]](/library/VEdGu70)

* <u>Prodromal</u> symptoms

* <u>Flu-like</u> symptoms (e.g., <u>fever</u>, <u>malaise</u>)

* <u>Pain</u>, <u>paresthesia</u>, and <u>pruritus</u> near the bite site





### Encephalitic rabies (∼ 80% of cases) [[2]](/library/srdtir0)




* Hydrophobia: Rabies patients experience involuntary, painful pharyngeal muscle spasms when trying to drink; later on in the disease, the sight of water alone may provoke <u>nausea</u> or <u>vomiting</u>.

* <u>CNS</u> symptoms

* <u>Anxiety</u>, <u>agitation</u>, and combativeness alternating with calm periods

* Confusion and <u>hallucinations</u>

* <u>Photophobia</u>

* <u>Fasciculations</u>

* <u>Seizures</u>

* ↑ Muscle tone and reflexes with <u>nuchal rigidity</u>

* Autonomic symptoms (e.g., <u>hypersalivation</u>, <u>hyperhidrosis</u>)

* <u>Coma</u> and <u>death</u> within days to weeks of the development of neurological symptoms





### Paralytic rabies (∼ 20% of cases) [[2]](/library/srdtir0)




* <u>Flaccid paralysis</u>, gradually ascending and spreading from bite wound  [[4]](/library/O0aITQ)

* <u>Paraplegia</u> and loss of sphincter tone

* <u>Respiratory failure</u> and <u>death</u>





> [!NOTE]
> The <u>pathognomonic</u> feature of rabies is <u>hydrophobia</u> due to pharyngeal muscle spasm. This may present along with <u>agitation</u>, strange behavior, mental status changes, and possibly foaming at the mouth.

---

## Diagnosis

Suspect rabies in patients with potential exposure and <u>clinical features of rabies</u>.




### Antemortem diagnosis [[2]](/library/srdtir0)




Several tests using multiple specimens must be performed because <u>virus</u> and <u>antibody</u> detection vary throughout disease. Identifying <u>rabies virus</u> <u>antigen</u> or <u>nucleic acid</u> confirms the diagnosis. [[2]](/library/srdtir0)




* Required specimens: serum, saliva, <u>CSF</u>, and <u>skin biopsy</u>  [[2]](/library/srdtir0)

* <u>Laboratory studies</u> [[2]](/library/srdtir0)

* <u>RT-PCR</u> to detect rabies <u>RNA</u>

* Cell culture to isolate <u>rabies virus</u>

* Direct <u>fluorescent antibody staining</u> for viral <u>antigen</u> in <u>skin biopsy</u>

* <u>Indirect fluorescent antibody testing</u>

* Serum <u>antibodies</u> detected in individuals who are not immunized and did not receive <u>rabies PEP</u> indicate a rabies infection

* <u>Antibodies</u> in the <u>CSF</u> regardless of the <u>immunization</u> history indicate a rabies infection

* <u>Virus</u> neutralization test

* Rabies CSF analysis: <u>lymphocytic</u> <u>pleocytosis</u>, ↑ protein, normal or ↑ <u>glucose</u> [[5]](/library/lGdvzr0)[[6]](/library/AN1Rdh0)





> [!TIP]
> If a case of rabies is suspected in the US, contact the state health department and <u>CDC</u> to determine if testing is necessary and what specimens are required.




### Postmortem diagnosis



* Postmortem <u>brain</u> tissue <u>autopsy</u>

* Immunofluorescent staining of viral <u>antigen</u> in infected <u>CNS</u> tissue

* Histopathological findings: Negri bodies (eosinophilic <u>cytoplasmic</u> <u>inclusion bodies</u> typically found in the <u>cerebellum</u> and <u>hippocampus</u>)

## Treatment

For management of individuals with potential rabies exposure, see “<u>Rabies PEP</u>.”




* Symptomatic rabies is almost universally fatal. [[2]](/library/srdtir0)

* Patients are managed with <u>palliative care</u> (e.g., <u>pain management</u>, sedation).

---

## Rabies preexposure prophylaxis

* Indications: individuals at increased risk of rabies exposure, e.g., [[6]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[7]](/library/KKdUhI0)

* <u>Occupational exposures</u> (e.g., veterinarians)

* Recreational exposures (e.g., spelunkers)

* Travelers to <u>endemic</u> areas

* <u>Immunization schedule</u>: See “<u>Vaccines before travel</u>.”





> [!WARNING]
> <u>Rabies PEP</u> is still required for patients exposed to rabies who previously received <u>rabies PrEP</u>. [[2]](/library/srdtir0)

---

## Rabies postexposure prophylaxis

Recommendations in this article are consistent with the <u>CDC</u> and <u>ACIP</u> guidelines for <u>rabies PEP</u>. [[8]](/library/M2WMRk0)[[9]](/library/oKd0hI0) Consider following the WHO guidelines for <u>rabies PEP</u> in resource-limited settings. [[10]](/library/UEdbE70)




### Approach [[6]](/library/AN1Rdh0)




* <u>Manage bite wounds</u> (e.g., with <u>irrigation</u>, <u>debridement</u>).

* Perform a <u>rabies risk assessment</u> based on the source and nature of exposure.

* Administer <u>rabies PEP</u> if required.

* Follow local protocols for animal observation, testing, and reporting requirements.

* Inform the patient when to return for subsequent rabies <u>vaccinations</u>.





### Rabies risk assessment [[6]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[8]](/library/M2WMRk0)




#### Wild <u>animal bites</u>




* High-risk animals (e.g., bats, raccoons, skunks, foxes, other carnivores) and monkeys

* Animal is not present: Administer <u>rabies PEP</u>.

* Animal is present: Contact the local health department for expedited animal rabies testing.

* Positive: Administer <u>rabies PEP</u>.

* Negative: No <u>rabies PEP</u> is necessary.

* If results cannot be obtained expeditiously, initiate <u>rabies PEP</u> and discontinue if negative.

* Low-risk animals (e.g., rodents, lagomorphs): No <u>rabies PEP</u> is necessary.





> [!WARNING]
> Any suspicion of a <u>bat bite</u> (e.g., waking up with a bat in the room) warrants the administration of <u>rabies PEP</u>, even if there is no evidence of a bite. [[2]](/library/srdtir0)




#### Domestic <u>animal bites</u>




* Dogs, cats, ferrets

* Animal is not present: Administer <u>rabies PEP</u>.

* Animal is present: Confine and observe the animal for 10 days.

* Animal becomes symptomatic

* Administer <u>rabies PEP</u>.

* Contact the local health department for expedited animal rabies testing.

* If animal rabies testing is negative, discontinue <u>rabies PEP</u>.

* Animal remains asymptomatic: No <u>rabies PEP</u> is necessary.

* Other domestic animals: Consult the local health department.





### <u>Rabies PEP</u> regimens [[2]](/library/srdtir0)




#### Unvaccinated patients [[6]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[8]](/library/M2WMRk0)[[9]](/library/oKd0hI0)




* Rabies immune globulin (RIG) DOSAGE [[2]](/library/srdtir0)

* Infiltrate as much RIG as feasible into and around the wound.

* Inject the remaining RIG at a site distant from the site of <u>vaccine</u> administration.

* PLUS inactivated rabies vaccine DOSAGE [[2]](/library/srdtir0)

* Administer on days 0, 3, 7, and 14.

* <u>Immunosuppressed</u> patients: Administer an additional dose on day 28.





> [!NOTE]
> Unvaccinated patients require <u>passive immunization</u> (i.e., RIG) and <u>active immunization</u> (i.e., <u>rabies vaccine</u>).




#### Vaccinated patients [[6]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[7]](/library/KKdUhI0)




An individual is considered vaccinated against rabies if they have previously completed <u>rabies PrEP</u>, <u>rabies PEP</u>, or they have partially completed the <u>rabies vaccination</u> series and have positive rabies <u>antibody</u> <u>titers</u>. [[2]](/library/srdtir0)




* Inactivated <u>rabies vaccine</u> DOSAGE on days 0 and 3 [[2]](/library/srdtir0)

* RIG is not required.
